title: Perimeter for Grade 3: How to Find the Distance Around Any Shape + Free Quiz
meta_title: Perimeter Grade 3: Find the Distance Around + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach perimeter to Grade 3 the clear way: add every side, use the rectangle and square shortcuts, then try a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Perimeter is just the walk around the edge of a shape. Here is how I explain it to eight-year-olds so it sticks — the shortcuts for squares and rectangles, missing-side puzzles, and a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Draw a rectangle on the board, tap each side once, and ask a Grade 3 class, ‘How far would an ant walk if it went all the way around and back to where it started?’ That single question is perimeter, and it lands far better than any definition. Perimeter for Grade 3 is nothing more than the total distance around the outside of a flat shape — you add up the length of every side, and the sum is the perimeter. No multiplication tricks required to begin with, just careful adding and a habit of not skipping a side.

The one mistake I see over and over is a child counting three sides of a rectangle and forgetting the fourth, or counting a corner twice. So the very first rule I teach is a physical one: put a small dot at one corner, then travel around the shape adding each side out loud, and stop the moment you reach your dot again. When you are back at the dot, you are done.

What perimeter really means at the Grade 3 level

Perimeter is a length, so it is always measured in length units — centimetres (cm) or metres (m) in most NCERT Class 3 work. If the sides of a shape are 3 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm, the perimeter is 3 + 5 + 3 + 5 = 16 cm. Notice the answer carries the unit ‘cm’. A perimeter with no unit is only half an answer, and I mark it as incomplete on purpose so children learn to write it every time.

Keep this separate in your mind from how much space is inside the shape — that is a different idea children meet a little later. Right now, we care only about the edge, the boundary, the walk around.

Adding up all the sides of an irregular shape

Irregular shapes are where the ‘add every side’ rule shows its worth, because no shortcut can rescue a child who forgets a side. Suppose a six-sided garden has edges of 4 m, 2 m, 3 m, 2 m, 1 m and 4 m. There is no clever formula — you simply add them all: 4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 16 m.

  • Start at one corner and mark it.
  • Write each side length as you go, in order, so none gets missed.
  • Add the list up carefully — group friendly pairs that make ten if it helps.
  • Write the unit (cm or m) after your total.

I actually teach irregular shapes before the shortcuts. When children learn the formulas first, they try to force every shape into a rectangle box in their head. Learning ‘just add the sides’ first keeps the real idea front and centre, and the shortcuts then feel like a well-earned reward.

The rectangle shortcut: add two sides, then double

A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides — two lengths and two widths. So instead of adding four numbers, a Grade 3 child can add the length and the width once, then double the result. For a rectangle 8 cm long and 3 cm wide: 8 + 3 = 11, and 11 × 2 = 22 cm. It matches 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 exactly, which is worth showing side by side so the shortcut feels honest rather than magic.

The square shortcut: multiply one side by four

A square is even friendlier because all four sides are equal. Measure one side and multiply by 4. A square tile with a side of 6 cm has a perimeter of 6 × 4 = 24 cm. This is a lovely early link to the times tables — children who know their 4-times table find square perimeters almost instant.

Finding a missing side

Once adding is solid, missing-side puzzles are the natural next step and children genuinely enjoy them. If a rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and one length is 6 cm, what is the width? Two lengths use up 6 + 6 = 12 cm, leaving 20 − 12 = 8 cm for the two widths, so each width is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm. It is a small piece of detective work, and it quietly builds the reversibility that later algebra depends on.

A quick comparison of the three methods

Irregular shapeadd up every side4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 4 m16 m

A simple routine that builds fluency

Ten minutes beats an hour. A pattern that works well: one day measuring real objects around the house with a ruler — a book cover, a floor tile, a photo frame — and finding their perimeters; the next day a few written questions mixing squares, rectangles and irregular shapes so the child has to decide which method fits. That deciding step is where the learning shows. One honest caveat: do not rush to the shortcuts. A child who can explain why (length + width) × 2 works is far ahead of one who has only memorised it and cannot say why the doubling is there.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly what we have gone through — adding all the sides, the square and rectangle shortcuts, units, and a missing-side question. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded perimeter questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Perimeter Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on finding the perimeter of squares, rectangles and irregular shapes. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What does the perimeter of a shape measure?
options: The distance all the way around the shape
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a flat shape. You add up the lengths of all the sides.

questions.q: A triangle has sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
A square has a side of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: All four sides are equal, so multiply one side by 4: 7 × 4 = 28 cm.

questions.q: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Add length and width, then double: (9 + 4) × 2 = 13 × 2 = 26 cm.

questions.q: Which unit should a perimeter answer use?
options: A length unit like cm or m
questions.explanation: Perimeter is a length, so it is written in length units such as centimetres (cm) or metres (m).

questions.q: An irregular shape has sides of 2 m, 5 m, 3 m and 6 m. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: There is no shortcut for irregular shapes; just add every side: 2 + 5 + 3 + 6 = 16 m.

questions.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm. One length is 6 cm. What is the width?
questions.explanation: The two lengths use 6 + 6 = 12 cm. That leaves 20 − 12 = 8 cm for the two widths, so each width is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.

questions.q: Which shape lets you find the perimeter by multiplying one side by 4?
questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides, so side × 4 gives its perimeter.

faq.q: What is perimeter in simple words for Grade 3?
faq.a: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a flat shape. You find it by adding up the length of every side, and the answer is written in a length unit like cm or m.

faq.q: How do you find the perimeter of a rectangle?
faq.a: Add the length and the width, then double the total — (length + width) × 2. For a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm that is (8 + 3) × 2 = 22 cm. It gives the same answer as adding all four sides.

faq.q: What is the shortcut for the perimeter of a square?
faq.a: Because all four sides of a square are equal, multiply one side by 4. A square with a side of 6 cm has a perimeter of 6 × 4 = 24 cm.

faq.q: How do you find a missing side when you know the perimeter?
faq.a: Subtract the sides you already know from the total perimeter; what is left belongs to the missing side or sides. For a rectangle, remember the two lengths and two widths come in equal pairs, so divide the remainder by 2.
